To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
magnetic resonance imaging can be used to design lateral treatment portals for patients who have locally advanced cervical cancer.

(a) conventional lateral portal design, based on anatomic landmarks, is suboptimal in 24% to 32% of patients with cervical cancer, and (b) the use of sagittal magnetic resonance images to design the lateral treatment portals is a simple, accurate, and cost-effective method to avoid the potential for suboptimal treatment.

the use of standard radiation portals for patients with bulky or advanced cervical cancer can result in a significant failure to encompass all of the gross cancer extensions, and that use of magnetic resonance imaging can assist in the design and placement of lateral treatment portals that are more likely to encompass gross cancer extensions.

the development and application of new imaging technologies to improve the quality of radiation treatment of gynecologic cancer.
the development of a new method for the analysis of the treatment of the patient.
the development and application of magnetic resonance imaging to the design of radiation treatment portals for locally advanced cervical carcinoma.

magnetic resonance imaging is a useful tool in designing lateral radiation portals for patients with cervical cancer, and that sagittal imaging provides the most valuable information in this regard.

the use of conventional lateral portals may result in a failure to treat gross disease, and that this is more common than is appreciated.
the lateral radiation portals should be designed based on the patient's sagittal anatomy, rather than on a "standard" or "conventional" lateral radiation portal design.
